newsitem.title: USA: Espy prober gets first setback; execs acquitted.
newsitem.headline: Espy prober gets first setback; execs acquitted.

text.p: Two former executives of the nation's second largest crop insurer were found not guilty Thursday of charges that they funnelled illegal campaign contributions to the brother of then Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy to win favour with the Clinton cabinet member.

The acquittal of former Crop Growers Corp. Chairman John Hemmingson and Senior Vice President Gary Black were the first major setbacks dealt to the criminal investigation of Espy that is being led by Independent Counsel Donald Smaltz.
Smaltz said in a statement he was disappointed with the jury's verdict but would "now move on to other aspects of our investigation."

In charges that arose out of his investigation of Espy, Hemmingson and Black were accused of defrauding the government by concealing more than $40,000 in corporate contributions made to Henry Espy in order to win his brother's favour and fatten their wallets.
Defence attorneys argued that the government's case lacked proof and that the two former executives acted in "good faith" that they were not doing anything wrong.

Hemmingson has been found guilty in a separate trial in New Orleans of laundering a $20,000 political contribution to Henry Espy, and last month the Crop Growers firm pleaded no contest to conspiring to defraud the Federal Election Commission and was fined $2 million.

Henry Espy unsuccessfully ran for his brother's congressional seat in 1993 after Mike Espy was appointed Agriculture Secretary. Henry Espy will go on trial this month in Oxford, Miss., on charges of making false statements to a bank and participating in the illegal contribution scheme.
Mike Espy has been under investigation since 1994 for allegedly accepting illegal gifts and favours while he was agriculture secretary from companies his department regulated.

Smaltz's aggressive investigation has yielded impressive results up to this point, bringing criminal indictments and charges against more than a dozen individuals and concerns and winning the conviction of the largest fruit cooperative in the nation for fraud and illegal gratuities to Mike Espy.
The investigation has been widely expected to lead to the indictment this year of the former Clinton cabinet member.

Government investigators have also focused on Espy's relationship with Tyson Foods, the Arkansas-based poultry giant, and legal experts said an indictment of the poultry company was possible. Its chairman Don Tyson has long had close ties to President Clinton, a former Arkansas governor.
